name: Edward IV of England
summary: Edward defended hereditary kingship through parliamentary recognition, military victory and divine sanction. He strengthened royal finance and patronage, used punishment and reconciliation against opponents, and pursued dynastic and territorial aims abroad.

sources.title: Proclamation against Margaret and the Lancastrian leaders, April 1471, in Rymer’s Foedera XI, pp. 709–714
sources.author: Edward IV; edited by Thomas Rymer
sources.usedFor: Royal arguments for legitimacy, armed restoration and sworn allegiance.

sources.title: Royal letter to John Pickering, 13 November 1478, in The York mercers and merchant adventurers, pp. 79–80
sources.author: Edward IV; edited by Maud Sellers (1918)
sources.usedFor: Personal intervention against discriminatory treatment of northern merchants.

sources.title: Taking the Throne: Justifications and Methods of Edward IV, including extracts from his 1475 will
sources.author: Dan Moorhouse
sources.usedFor: Succession provisions and the distinction between royal claims and other Yorkist propaganda.

sources.title: Edward IV: the construction of a royal reputation, doctoral thesis (2017)
sources.author: Andrew Robert Whittle, University of East Anglia
sources.usedFor: Critical comparison of chronicles; royal foreign policy, Clarence and merchant privileges.

sources.title: York and Tudor England, ORB textbook (1999)
sources.author: Steven Muhlberger
sources.usedFor: Royal finance, patronage, reconciliation and succession.

sources.title: Edward IV, Dictionary of National Biography (1889)
sources.author: James Gairdner
sources.usedFor: Career chronology, personally prosecuted treason, military decisions and Scottish treaty.

sources.title: Edward IV to Clarence, Warwick and the Archbishop of York, 9 July 1469, letter 719, The Paston Letters V
sources.author: Edward IV; edited by James Gairdner
sources.usedFor: The king’s own correspondence asserting personal commands and allegiance.

sources.author: David Grummitt, History of Parliament Trust
sources.usedFor: Distinguishes the king’s decisions from Alcock’s parliamentary rhetoric and followers’ motives.

notes: Coverage spans accession, the 1469–1471 crises, restoration, the French settlement, Clarence’s prosecution and the final Scottish campaign. The medieval record yields few answers to modern policy questions. Later narrative reports receive medium confidence at most; uncertain stories about particular murders are not treated as direct admissions. Formal royal assent and policies merely advocated by ministers do not establish personal views. Royal favour to merchants and the 1478 corrective letter are recorded as mixed evidence, not a general free-trade doctrine. No historical inferences were added. The full statement list was reviewed against downloaded primary texts and scholarship; unsupported questions remain null.
